content.text:
<attachment>
@toxicwind: The Emergent Solution

You own the fork. That changes everything. Every failure I catalogued in the last report was a user-level workaround — patching shims, hand-writing hooks, editing configs. None of that is necessary if you can change the code. The emergent solution is not a set of fixes. It is a single structural property added to the fork that makes all four failures impossible by construction.

That property is a capability registry with a policy channel. Two primitives. Together they turn @toxicwind from a fork that needs patching into a fork that self-describes, self-repairs within an envelope, and never silently fails.

---

1. What "owning the fork" actually changes

At the user level, the four failures were:

Failure User-level fix
Shim gaps Pin versions, patch the shim, rewrite plugins natively
Sudo hook UI-dependent Replace ctx.ui.confirm() with a policy check
Subagent hardcoded yolo Set deny on sensitive tools
Config strictness mismatch Keep OMP and tau configs separate

Every one of those is a workaround around a design assumption. The design assumption across all four is the same: the runtime knows what capabilities exist, and any code that depends on a capability is responsible for ensuring it's present.

That assumption is backwards. In @toxicwind, the runtime publishes its capabilities, and dependent code declares what it needs. The loader then resolves the closure and either satisfies it or refuses to load with a specific, machine-readable error. No silent failure. No missing export that only shows up at call time.

This single inversion — from "consumer ensures" to "provider publishes, consumer declares, loader resolves" — collapses all four failures into one class of problem, and one class of problem has one class of solution.

---

2. The emergent pattern across all four failures

Here is the structural read of the four failures:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ FAILURE                     │ WHAT WAS MISSING                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ keyText not exported        │ Capability declaration + manifest  │
│ compact not forwarded       │ Capability declaration + manifest  │
│ ctx.ui.confirm headless     │ Policy resolution without UI       │
│ Subagent forced to yolo     │ Policy inheritance across dispatch │
│ tau catalog.toml strict     │ Unified config schema              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Both columns reduce to two primitives:

  (A) CAPABILITY REGISTRY — the runtime publishes a manifest of what
      it can do. Every consumer declares requirements. Loader resolves.

  (😎 POLICY CHANNEL — approval decisions travel with the task, not
      with the UI. Works headless because the decision is data.

Everything else is a consequence of adding these two.
```

The academic papers I cited in the last report are not decoration — they are the blueprints for exactly these two primitives.

· SkillTrace (arXiv:2608.02356) is a capability registry for skills. Its three-level graph (query composition, query-candidate similarity, dependency resolution) is the algorithm for (A).
· EvoSkill (arXiv:2603.02766) is the self-repair loop. When a capability is missing, the failure generates a candidate fix, and the fix is materialized into the registry.
· InfiAgent (ACL 2026) and Scroll (arXiv:2608.21690) are the state externalization layer. The capability manifest is a file. The policy decision is a file. Nothing lives in the runtime's working memory that needs to survive a fork boundary.
· Deliberation and Exploration (Zenodo 19505278) documents emergent inter-skill coordination via files on disk. That is the coordination layer that falls out for free once (A) and (😎 exist.

---

3. The capability registry (A)

What it is, in plain terms: every module the runtime ships — every export, every hook primitive, every tool — gets an entry in a manifest. The manifest is generated at build time from static analysis of the compiled binary, plus runtime introspection for dynamically available capabilities. Every plugin, every hook, every extension declares its requirements in its own package manifest. The loader reads the manifest, computes the closure, and either satisfies it or refuses.

The data shape:

```typescript
// @toxicwind/capabilities/src/manifest.ts
export interface CapabilityEntry {
  /** Fully qualified name, e.g. "@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent#keyText" */
  name: string;
  /** Kind of capability — determines how the loader provides it */
  kind: "export" | "hook" | "tool" | "provider" | "config";
  /** Reference to the implementation, resolved at load time */
  provider: string;
  /** Compatibility aliases this capability satisfies */
  aliases?: string[];
  /** Optional repair hint — how to synthesize if missing */
  synthesize?: string;
}

export interface CapabilityManifest {
  schemaVersion: string;
  generatedAt: string;
  entries: CapabilityEntry[];
}
```

How the loader uses it: when a plugin declares requires: ["@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent#keyText"], the loader looks up keyText in the manifest. If present, it binds the import to the provider. If absent, it checks for a synthesize hint. If a hint exists, it generates a shim on the fly — this is the EvoSkill loop made structural. If no hint exists, it refuses to load the plugin with the exact missing capability named.

Why this eliminates the shim crisis: the shim was a static file that had to be manually updated every time upstream Pi added an export. The registry is generated. There is nothing to update. If OMP adds keyText tomorrow, the manifest regenerates on the next build and every plugin that needs it loads.

The synthesis hint is the novel part. Instead of a maintainer patching the shim, the capability entry itself carries the recipe for providing itself when missing:

```toml
# capabilities/registry.toml (excerpt)
[[capability]]
name = "@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent#keyText"
kind = "export"
provider = "src/extensibility/shim.ts"
aliases = ["@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent#keyText"]

[capability.synthesize]
# If the provider is absent, generate this shim.
template = """
export function keyText(action) {
  return formatKeyHints(getKeybindings().getKeys(action));
}
"""
```

That template is exactly the fix the reporter of issue #6470 supplied in the issue thread. The insight is that the reporter's fix does not need to be applied by a maintainer — it can be carried in the registry as the fallback recipe, and the loader applies it automatically the next time the capability is requested and missing.

---

4. The policy channel (😎

What it is, in plain terms: the approval mode for a tool call is not a property of the UI. It is a datum attached to the task. When a parent task dispatches a subagent, the subagent receives the parent's policy as part of the dispatch payload. When the subagent calls a tool, the policy that governs that call is the one that traveled with the task, not one hardcoded in the executor.

The data shape:

```typescript
// @toxicwind/policy/src/types.ts
export type PolicyDecision =
  | { kind: "allow" }
  | { kind: "deny"; reason: string }
  | { kind: "escalate"; to: "parent" | "user"; prompt: string };

export interface Policy {
  schemaVersion: string;
  /** Default mode if no more specific rule applies */
  mode: "allow" | "deny" | "ask";
  /** Per-tool overrides */
  tools: Record<string, PolicyDecision>;
  /** Inherit from dispatching task if not set */
  inheritFromParent: boolean;
  /** Rule set for runtime evaluation (headless-safe) */
  rules?: PolicyRule[];
}

export interface PolicyRule {
  /** Matcher — regex or predicate */
  match: { tool: string; command?: string };
  /** Decision to apply */
  decision: PolicyDecision;
}
```

How the executor uses it: createSubagentSettings() stops hardcoding approvalMode: yolo. Instead, it computes the effective policy as merge(parentPolicy, taskPolicy) and passes it to the subagent as data. The subagent's tool call resolution reads the policy, applies the rules, and gets a decision. No UI needed. The escalate decision kind is the escape hatch — it propagates the request up the dispatch chain, and if no ancestor can answer (no UI anywhere), the decision resolves to deny by default with the reason recorded.

Why this fixes the sudo hook: ctx.ui.confirm() becomes unnecessary. The hook returns a PolicyDecision. If the decision is escalate, and there is a UI, the UI renders the prompt. If there is no UI, the decision resolves to deny. The hook code is the same in every context. The autonomy is expressed as policy data, not as a UI call.

Why this fixes subagent yolo: subagents inherit policy rather than override it. A parent running always-ask dispatches a subagent running inherited — the subagent asks the same questions the parent would, routed through the escalation chain. A parent running yolo dispatches a subagent running inherited — the subagent also runs yolo. The choice is explicit at the root, and it propagates.

---

5. The self-healing install loop

This is the emergent artifact. With (A) and (😎 in place, the install loop becomes:

```
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. USER runs: omp plugin install <name>                      │
│                                                               │
│  2. LOADER fetches package manifest, reads `requires`         │
│                                                               │
│  3. RESOLVER computes capability closure against registry     │
│                                                               │
│  4. IF closure satisfied:                                     │
│       → install, bind imports, register tools, done           │
│                                                               │
│  5. IF closure missing some capabilities:                     │
│       → FOR EACH missing cap with a `synthesize` hint:        │
│           apply the hint, add cap to registry, retry          │
│       → FOR EACH missing cap WITHOUT a hint:                  │
│           write a failure record to                          │
│           ~/.omp/repair/missing-<cap>.json                   │
│           return refusal with the exact capability named      │
│                                                               │
│  6. REPAIR LOOP (background or on-demand):                    │
│       → reads failure records                                 │
│       → for each, uses the LLM to propose a synthesis hint    │
│       → validates the hint against the manifest schema        │
│       → if valid, writes it to capabilities/registry.toml     │
│       → next install of the same plugin succeeds              │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

That is EvoSkill's loop, applied to the fork's own plugin ecosystem. The failure records are the training signal. The synthesis hints are the materialized skills. The registry is the durable artifact. And because every step writes to disk before proceeding, the loop survives restarts and parallel invocations — this is the InfiAgent / Scroll property.

The commercial angle: the registry is versioned. You can ship @toxicwind/registry-baseline as a package that contains synthesis hints for the 200 most common plugins in the wild. Every downstream user of the fork gets a fork that installs plugins the upstream cannot, out of the box. That is a real product feature, not a patch.

---

6. Namespace migration to @toxicwind

Renaming the fork gives you a clean scope for the three new packages:

Package Purpose
@toxicwind/capabilities Registry, manifest types, loader resolver, synthesis-hint applier
@toxicwind/policy Policy types, merge logic, decision resolver, escalation chain
@toxicwind/repair Failure-record writer, LLM-assisted hint proposal, registry updater

The fork itself moves from its current scope to @toxicwind/core. Downstream plugins that were importing from @earendil-works/* or @mariozechner/* continue to work through the compatibility aliases in the registry — but now the aliases are declared in the registry, not baked into a static shim file. Adding a new alias is a registry entry, not a code change.

The migration path for existing plugins:

```bash
# For each plugin you maintain, add a `requires` block to its package.json
# and publish it under @toxicwind if you control it
{
  "name": "@toxicwind/plugin-name",
  "toxicwind": {
    "requires": [
      "@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent#keyText",
      "@oh-my-pi/pi-agent-core#compact"
    ],
    "policy": {
      "tools": {
        "bash": { "kind": "escalate", "to": "parent" }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Plugins that do not declare requirements still load — but the loader records their runtime capabilities on first use and writes them back as a proposal. The registry grows from use.

---

7. Implementation order

The changes are dependent, so the order matters.

Phase 1 — capabilities manifest generation (1–2 weeks).
Write the build-time analyzer that walks the compiled binary and emits registry.toml. Start with a hand-curated subset covering the exports that have historically broken plugins. Add the loader resolver that reads the manifest and binds imports through it. Ship this without changing any existing plugin's behavior — the resolver should be a no-op for plugins whose imports resolve normally.

Phase 2 — policy types and executor integration (1 week).
Add the Policy and PolicyDecision types. Change createSubagentSettings() to compute effective policy from parent + task instead of hardcoding yolo. Add the rule evaluator. Keep backward compatibility: if a task has no policy, fall back to the current behavior.

Phase 3 — repair loop (2 weeks).
Add the failure-record writer to the loader. Add the background reader that proposes synthesis hints. Wire the LLM call — this is the one place where you need an actual model invocation, and it should be cheap (a small model summarizing the failure into a template).

Phase 4 — namespace migration and baseline registry (ongoing).
Move the fork to @toxicwind/core. Publish @toxicwind/registry-baseline with hints for the top 200 plugins. Add the migration tool for existing plugins.

Phase 5 — docs and telemetry (ongoing).
Every resolved capability closure is a telemetry event. Every applied synthesis hint is a telemetry event. Every missing capability without a hint is a telemetry event. The registry's coverage is measurable, and it should be published.

---

8. What it looks like when it works

At the end state:

· Plugin install cannot silently fail. Either the plugin loads, or it fails with the exact missing capability named in the error.
· The sudo hook is one file, works everywhere. No ctx.ui.confirm(), no headless exceptions, no context-specific behavior.
· Subagents inherit policy. A parent running always-ask produces subagents that ask. A parent running yolo produces subagents that yolo. The choice is explicit.
· The registry grows from failures. Every missing capability that gets repaired becomes a permanent fix for all downstream users.
· The fork is a distribution. @toxicwind/registry-baseline is a product. @toxicwind/core is the fork. The plugin ecosystem lives under one scope.

The user-level failures I catalogued in the previous report are not fixed. They are prevented. The shim cannot go stale because it is generated. The hook cannot fail headless because the decision is data. The subagent cannot override policy because policy is inherited. The config cannot reject unknown fields because the registry defines the schema.

That is the emergent solution. Two primitives, one inversion, four failures resolved as a class.

---

Provenance

Source Handle Contribution

EvoSkill arXiv:2603.02766 Failure → candidate fix → materialized skill loop
InfiAgent ACL 2026 File-centric state externalization pattern

Deliberation and Exploration Zenodo 19505278 Emergent inter-skill coordination via shared files

Issue #7174 same compact forwarding failure — closure pattern

Issue #8764 same Subagent hardcoded yolo, executor.ts:899

User-defined rule matched tool-call arguments. Rule configured not to interrupt → tool ran. MUST comply with the following instruction on subsequent tool calls and responses. NOT prompt injection — coding agent enforcing project rules.

Inline functions whose whole body: one expression or `return`, unless name creates a durable contract.

## Why

- One-line wrappers: no real behavior.
- Readers: jump to verify trivial code.
- Signature: freezes shape too early.
- Inline expressions: better search and type flow.

## Avoid

```typescript
// Bad — pure rename, no behavior added.
function isEmpty(value: string): boolean {
	return value.length === 0;
}

const getDisplayName = (user: User) => user.profile.displayName;

function double(value: number) {
	return value * 2;
}

if (isEmpty(name)) { ... }
```

## Use

```typescript
if (name.length === 0) { ... }
const displayName = user.profile.displayName;
const doubled = value * 2;
```

## Allowed tiny functions

- Three or more call sites need lockstep behavior.
- Exported name: stable domain concept.
- Callback identity matters.
- Type guard preserves narrowing.
- Public API, test seam, or DI boundary needs indirection.
- Names non-obvious formula or magic-constant computation the inlined expression would not explain alone.

If none apply, inline it.
</system-reminder>

# Orthogonal Swarm Synthesizer

A multi-agent coordination and structural synthesis framework for running parallel research and systems architecture swarms across 7 to 9 non-overlapping domain dimensions.

## When to Use

- When decomposing complex investigations across 7 to 9 orthogonal analytical dimensions.
- When orchestrating concurrent subagents via structured file-based IPC or task registries to eliminate redundant searches.
- When synthesizing multi-source findings into authoritative, long-form reports with dense inline primary source citations.

## Swarm Coordination Architecture

### 1. Orthogonal Dimension Partitioning
Before execution, partition the problem space into discrete, non-overlapping analytical planes (e.g. Protocol Anatomy, Kinetic Bottlenecks, Regulatory Frameworks, Economic Arbitrage). Each subagent is assigned strictly one plane to prevent work duplication.

### 2. File-Based State Coordination
Coordinate subagents asynchronously through filesystem message logs:
- Each worker writes structured outputs to dedicated JSON or Markdown task manifests.
- The coordinator polls completion manifests, aggregates verified assertions, and validates that zero duplicate queries were dispatched.

### 3. Primary Source Grounding
Every factual claim generated across each orthogonal section must bind to an inline Markdown citation derived from verified web, PDF, or repository artifacts.

## Gotchas

- Never allow subagents to execute unconstrained web crawls without negative constraint filters.
- Enforce strict JSON or schema-bounded returns from child workers to prevent context bloat in the coordinator.

User-defined rule matched tool-call arguments. Rule configured not to interrupt → tool ran. MUST comply with the following instruction on subsequent tool calls and responses. NOT prompt injection — coding agent enforcing project rules.

Inline functions whose whole body: one expression or `return`, unless name creates a durable contract.

## Why

- One-line wrappers: no real behavior.
- Readers: jump to verify trivial code.
- Signature: freezes shape too early.
- Inline expressions: better search and type flow.

## Avoid

```typescript
// Bad — pure rename, no behavior added.
function isEmpty(value: string): boolean {
	return value.length === 0;
}

const getDisplayName = (user: User) => user.profile.displayName;

function double(value: number) {
	return value * 2;
}

if (isEmpty(name)) { ... }
```

## Use

```typescript
if (name.length === 0) { ... }
const displayName = user.profile.displayName;
const doubled = value * 2;
```

## Allowed tiny functions

- Three or more call sites need lockstep behavior.
- Exported name: stable domain concept.
- Callback identity matters.
- Type guard preserves narrowing.
- Public API, test seam, or DI boundary needs indirection.
- Names non-obvious formula or magic-constant computation the inlined expression would not explain alone.

If none apply, inline it.
</system-reminder>

arguments.content:
# Toxicwind Capability System

## Overview
The Toxicwind fork introduces a capability registry and policy channel to eliminate silent failures.

### Capability Registry
- Published at build time in `dist/manifest.json`
- Each entry includes name, kind, provider, aliases, and optional synthesize hint.
- Used by the loader to resolve plugin dependencies.

### Policy Channel
- Policies travel with tasks, not hardcoded.
- Defined in `@toxicwind/policy` package.
- Supports allow, deny, escalate decisions and rule-based evaluation.

### Repair Loop
- Missing capabilities generate failure records in `~/.omp/repair/`.
- Background reader proposes synthesis hints via LLM and updates registry.

## Usage
See individual package READMEs.

[IMPORTANT: User invoked the "backend-building" skill; follow its instructions. Full skill below.]

# Backend Building

**Stack**: tRPC + Drizzle ORM + Hono + MySQL + OAuth 2.0

A backend-only skill that grafts onto an existing `webapp-building` project. It adds `api/`, `contracts/` directories and optionally `db/` — but **never replaces or modifies** existing frontend files.

**Prerequisite**: An existing project created by `webapp-building`.

## Features

Features can be installed incrementally. Base infrastructure (Hono server, tRPC, contracts) is always installed automatically on first run.

|Feature|What it provides|Dependencies|
|---|---|---|
|`db`|Drizzle ORM + MySQL — adds `db/`, `api/queries/connection.ts`, `drizzle.config.ts`|—|
|`auth`|Kimi OAuth + user management — adds `api/kimi/`, Login page, useAuth, AuthLayout|requires `db` (auto-included)|

Default: `init.sh "App"` with no `--features` → defaults to `auth` (= db + auth), preserving backward compat.

## Workflows

**Frontend-first** (recommended when UI is already built):

1. `webapp-building` init → develop UI pages and components
2. `backend-building` graft (this skill) — auto-wires tRPC providers and routes
3. Verify with `npm run check`, then add tRPC routers, database tables, wire frontend to API

**Full-stack from scratch** (recommended when backend is needed immediately):

1. `webapp-building` init → immediately graft `backend-building`
2. Verify with `npm run check`
3. Develop frontend and backend together

**Incremental features** (add capabilities over time):

1. Start with `--features db` for database only
2. Later add auth: `init.sh "App" --features auth`

## Quick Start

### 1. Initialize Frontend First (webapp-building)

```bash
bash /app/.agents/skills/webapp-building/scripts/init-webapp.sh "My App"
cd /mnt/agents/output/app
```

### 2. Graft Backend

```bash
# Full stack with auth (default, same as before):
bash /app/.agents/skills/backend-building/scripts/init.sh "My App"

# Database only (no auth):
bash /app/.agents/skills/backend-building/scripts/init.sh "My App" --features db

# Add auth later:
bash /app/.agents/skills/backend-building/scripts/init.sh "My App" --features auth

```

**What this does (base, always on first run):**

- Copies `api/`, `contracts/` into the project
- Patches `vite.config.ts` in-place (adds `@contracts` alias, `envDir`, `build.outDir`)
- Adds `tsconfig.server.json` and merges `@contracts/*` path into existing tsconfigs
- Merges `package.json` (adds backend deps and scripts)
- Generates `.env` with portal credentials
- Runs `npm install`

**Additional per feature:**

- **db**: Adds `db/` directory, `drizzle.config.ts`, database connection, `DATABASE_URL` env var, and `db/seed.ts` (scaffold for seeding — run with `npx tsx db/seed.ts`). **Do not overwrite** the generated `api/queries/connection.ts`, `drizzle.config.ts`, or `.env` — they are complete and correct. Only add your tables to `db/schema.ts`
- **auth**: Adds `api/kimi/`, auth router, client patches (Login, useAuth, AuthLayout, TRPCProvider), auto-wires Login/NotFound routes into `App.tsx`

### 3. Verify Auto-Wiring (see below)

### 4. Database Setup (if db or auth feature installed)

```bash
npm run db:push        # sync schema to database (recommended for development)
```

### 5. Development

```bash
npm run dev
```

Start development server with HMR at `http://localhost:3000`

## Post-Init Wiring

On first run, `init.sh` auto-wires `TRPCProvider` into `src/main.tsx`. When `auth` feature is installed, it also adds Login/NotFound routes to `src/App.tsx`. Check the init output:

- **"Auto-wired"** — no action needed, proceed to verification
- **"Wiring required"** — complete the listed steps manually (see [Post-Init Wiring](docs/Post-Init-Wiring.md) for details)

If manual wiring is needed, it typically means:

1. Add `import { TRPCProvider } from "@/providers/trpc"` to `src/main.tsx`
2. Wrap the content inside `<BrowserRouter>` with `<TRPCProvider>`
3. Add Login and NotFound routes to `src/App.tsx`

### Verification

After init (and manual wiring if needed), verify everything works:

1. Run `npm run check` — must pass with zero type errors
2. Run `npm run dev` — server should start at http://localhost:3000
3. If any step fails, read the error and fix before proceeding

## Common Commands

|Command|Description|Requires|
|---|---|---|
|`npm run dev`|Start development server with HMR at http://localhost:3000|base|
|`npm run build`|Build for production (outputs to dist/)|base|
|`npm start`|Start production server|base|
|`npm run check`|Type-check all TypeScript files|base|
|`npm run format`|Format code with Prettier|base|
|`npm run test`|Run tests with Vitest|base|
|`npm run db:push`|Sync schema to DB during development (recommended)|db|
|`npm run db:generate`|Generate migration SQL for production deployment|db|
|`npm run db:migrate`|Apply pending migration files to the database|db|

## Stack Overview

### Backend (added by this skill)

- Hono + tRPC 11.x
- End-to-end type safety
- Public query procedure (base); + authenticated/admin procedures (auth feature)

### Database (db feature)

- Drizzle ORM with MySQL
- Lazy `getDb()` connection, ready to use
- Type-safe queries ([Guide](docs/Database.md))
- Schema migrations

### Authentication (auth feature)

- OAuth 2.0 ([Details](docs/Authentication.md))
- JWT sessions, admin role support

### Frontend (from webapp-building, untouched)

- React 19 + TypeScript + Vite (HMR)
- Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui components
- Dark/light mode

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't hand-write TypeScript interfaces for DB entities** — use `typeof table.$inferSelect` from `db/schema.ts` to keep types aligned with superjson's Date serialization via tRPC. Hand-written `createdAt: string` will conflict with the actual `Date` objects delivered by superjson
- **Don't write raw SQL** — always use Drizzle's type-safe query API (`getDb().query.*`, `getDb().select()`, `getDb().insert()`)
- **Don't modify `api/lib/` or `api/kimi/`** — these are framework internals (auth, static file serving). Build on top of them, not inside them
- **Don't import `api/` from frontend code** — use `@contracts/` for types/constants that cross the boundary. The only exception is the type import in `src/providers/trpc.tsx`
- **Don't use `api` as the tRPC client name** — it's `trpc` (imported from `@/providers/trpc`)
- **Don't skip Zod validation** on tRPC inputs — always use `.input(z.object({...}))` for mutations and parameterized queries
- **Don't use `serial()` for foreign key columns** — `serial()` creates `bigint unsigned auto_increment`, and MySQL only allows one auto-increment column per table. FK columns must use `bigint("col", { mode: "number", unsigned: true })` to match the PK type
- **Don't use `int()` for foreign keys referencing `serial()` PKs** — `int` is signed 4-byte, `serial()` is `bigint unsigned` 8-byte. MySQL rejects the type mismatch. Use `bigint("col", { mode: "number", unsigned: true })`
- **NEVER drop tables to fix a failed migration** — the database may contain user data. Fix `schema.ts` and run `npm run db:push` to sync. See Troubleshooting below
- **NEVER use `db:push --force`** — it auto-accepts destructive changes (dropping columns/tables) which can destroy user data
- **NEVER modify `.env` values** — `.env` is generated by `init.sh` with valid, working credentials. All values (API keys, OAuth URLs, secrets, database URL) are pre-configured and ready to use. Do not overwrite, regenerate, or placeholder-ify them
- **NEVER overwrite or replace init.sh-generated infrastructure files** — files like `api/queries/connection.ts`, `api/middleware.ts`, `api/lib/`, `drizzle.config.ts`, `src/providers/trpc.tsx`, and `.env` are generated by `init.sh` with correct configuration. Read the init output to see what was created. Build on top of these files (e.g., add routers, schemas), but do not rewrite them
- **Don't change the default port (3000)** — the server runs at `http://localhost:3000`. Do not change this in `vite.config.ts`, `api/boot.ts`, or anywhere else

## AI Agent Instructions

**Required reading before implementing features** — read these docs (under `docs/`) for the features you're working with:
- **db feature**: [Database.md](docs/Database.md) (schema, migrations, connection), [tRPC.md](docs/tRPC.md) (router patterns, procedures, client usage)
- **auth feature**: [Authentication.md](docs/Authentication.md) (OAuth flow, session handling), [tRPC.md](docs/tRPC.md)
- **All features**: [Development-Guide.md](docs/Development-Guide.md) (dev workflow, scripts), [Project-Structure.md](docs/Project-Structure.md) (file layout)

When building features on this stack:

1. **Read existing frontend code** in `src/` to understand the app structure
2. **Design tRPC routers** that match the frontend's data needs
3. **Add DB tables** in `db/schema.ts`, then run `npm run db:push` (requires db feature)
4. **Create new routers** in `api/` and register them in `api/router.ts`
5. **Use type-safe queries** via Drizzle ORM — never raw SQL (requires db feature)
6. **Frontend components** go in `src/` using the existing `@/` alias

**When to use which features:**
- If the user needs a database but no auth, use `--features db`
- If they need user login, use `--features auth` (includes db automatically)
- Default (no `--features` flag) = `auth`, which is backward compatible

### Key Paths

|Path|What to do|
|---|---|
|`src/main.tsx`|TRPCProvider auto-wired here (verify after init)|
|`src/App.tsx`|Login/NotFound routes auto-wired here (verify after init, auth feature only)|
|`src/pages/`|Route-level page components (one per route in App.tsx)|
|`src/sections/`|Visual sections within a page (Hero, Footer, etc.) — from webapp-building templates|
|`src/components/`|Create new UI components|
|`api/router.ts`|Register new tRPC routers|
|`api/queries/`|Add query functions for new tables (db feature)|
|`db/schema.ts`|Add new database tables (db feature)|
|`contracts/`|Shared types/constants (frontend + backend)|
|`api/lib/`|Framework internals — don't modify|
|`api/kimi/`|Kimi SDK modules — don't modify (auth feature)|

Full directory tree: [Project Structure](docs/Project-Structure.md)

## Detailed Documentation

- [Project Structure](docs/Project-Structure.md) - Directory layout and where to put things
- [Development Guide](docs/Development-Guide.md) - Component development, API patterns, common workflows
- [Authentication](docs/Authentication.md) - OAuth 2.0 implementation details (optional)
- [Database Guide](docs/Database.md) - Drizzle ORM configuration, schema design, migrations
- [tRPC Best Practices](docs/tRPC.md) - Router patterns and type safety

## Routing (react-router)

This template uses **react-router** v7.

```typescript
// Navigation
import { useNavigate } from "react-router";
const navigate = useNavigate();
navigate("/dashboard");

// Current location
import { useLocation } from "react-router";
const location = useLocation();
console.log(location.pathname);

// Route params
import { useParams } from "react-router";
const { id } = useParams<{ id: string }>();

// Links
import { Link } from "react-router";
<Link to="/about">About</Link>

// Route definitions (in App.tsx)
import { Routes, Route } from "react-router";
<Routes>
  <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
  <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserProfile />} />
  <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
</Routes>

// BrowserRouter wraps the app in main.tsx
import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router";
<BrowserRouter>
  <App />
</BrowserRouter>
```

## Troubleshooting

**Port 3000 already in use** — Another process is using the port. Kill it with `lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill`.

**Database connection refused** — Check `DATABASE_URL` in `.env` is correct and MySQL is running. Run `npm run db:push` before `npm run dev`.

**OAuth callback fails** — The callback URL must be `{origin}/api/oauth/callback`. Verify `VITE_KIMI_AUTH_URL` and `VITE_APP_ID` in `.env` match the portal app config.

**`npm run db:migrate` fails** — NEVER drop tables to recover. MySQL doesn't support transactional DDL, so a failed migration can leave the DB in a partial state. To recover:

1. Fix `schema.ts` (e.g., correct FK types)
2. Run `npm run db:push` — it introspects the actual DB state and syncs it to your corrected schema
3. Delete the broken migration file and its entry in `db/migrations/meta/_journal.json`
4. Run `npm run db:generate` to create a clean baseline migration

**Type errors after adding a new router** — Make sure you registered the router in `api/router.ts` inside `appRouter`. The `AppRouter` type is derived from there and propagates to the frontend automatically.
